extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and life-sciences attorneys (PTAB/IPR/PGR practitioners, challengers and patent owners)
extracted.subtask_short: PGR outcomes analysis for life sciences
extracted.subtask_description: A data-driven survey and comparative analysis of Post-Grant Review (PGR) outcomes (and comparisons to IPRs and district-court §112 outcomes) with an emphasis on biotechnology and pharmaceutical patents. Intended to inform practitioner decision-making about whether and how to pursue PGRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR filing eligibility and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: PGRs are only available for patent applications filed after March 16, 2013 and must be filed within nine months of patent grant or reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constraint (availability only for certain patents and a 9-month filing window) limits the pool of patents subject to PGR and can explain why fewer PGRs have been filed compared to IPRs. Timing can affect whether a biosimilar manufacturer or other challenger is in a position to file and can affect appellate standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR vs PGR statutory scope of invalidity challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs are limited to 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103 based on patents and printed publications; PGRs can include challenges under §§ 101, 102, 103, 112, and double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The broader scope in PGRs permits more types of attacks (e.g., §112 written description/enablement/indefiniteness and §101), but also introduces additional complexity and evidentiary burdens to develop the record across many possible grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel breadth and risk in PGRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Because PGRs allow a broader scope of invalidity challenges, they pose a greater risk of a broader scope of estoppel compared to IPRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners are estopped in district court and the ITC from raising grounds and prior art that were raised or could reasonably have been raised during post-grant proceedings; petitioners must therefore consider estoppel risk when deciding whether to file a PGR and which grounds to pursue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution rate as a key outcome metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution rates measure whether the PTAB institutes a petition (e.g., overall PGR institution rate 48% vs. IPR 65% in the data set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution rates vary by technology and challenge type and drive the overall practical risk to patent owners; lower institution rates in PGRs mean patent owners fare better overall in PGRs relative to IPRs, even if FWD invalidation rates (conditional on institution) are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology/category differences (TC 1600, Orange Book, Biologics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution and outcome metrics should be analyzed by technology subset: TC 1600 (biotech/chemistry), Orange Book-listed small-molecule drug patents, and biologic drug patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report finds TC 1600 PGRs instituted at similar rates to all PGRs (~50%), while Orange Book and biologic drug PGRs were instituted less frequently (23% and 40% respectively), but sample sizes for life-sciences subsets are small and trends may change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-limited evidentiary burden for PGRs
rubrics_metrics.description: The nine-month PGR filing window constrains petitioners' ability to gather prior art and expert evidence across a broader set of PGR-available challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This time limitation may increase the resources required to meet institution requirements for PGRs (broader prior art collection, more expert testimony) and is a possible reason for lower PGR institution rates compared to IPRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural denial bases (NHK–Fintiv and other procedural grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing basis for PGR (and IPR) denials are procedural reasons such as discretionary denial under 324(a), denials under 325(d), and denials tied to NHK–Fintiv factors considering parallel district-court proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since 2019 PTAB has increasingly used these procedural denials; NHK and Fintiv (and their factor-based analysis) can result in discretionary denials when there is advanced parallel litigation. These procedural practices have been controversial and subject to potential statutory/regulatory change, affecting future institution rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution rates by invalidity challenge type
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution rates should be tracked separately for challenges under §§ 101, 102, 103, and for §112 subtypes (indefiniteness, written description, enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the data, §103 challenges were most frequent (~80% of petitions). PGR institution rates in the sample ranged ~36–46% by challenge type (lowest for §101 at 36% in this data). When multiple challenge types exist in a petition each is reviewed separately for institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Written Decision (FWD) outcomes distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: FWD outcomes are categorized as all claims unpatentable, some claims unpatentable, or no claims unpatentable; PGR FWD invalidation of all claims was similar to IPRs (about 64% vs 62% in the samples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing FWD outcomes indicates that, conditional on institution and reaching FWD, PGRs and IPRs have similar rates of invalidating all claims. However, fewer PGRs reach institution, affecting aggregate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: FWD outcomes by invalidity challenge type
rubrics_metrics.description: Success at FWD varies by statute: §§101, 102, and §112 (written description/enablement) had relatively high rates (53–73%) of invalidating all challenged claims, while §112 indefiniteness (23%) and §103 (44%) were less likely to invalidate all claims in the sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because petitions often assert multiple grounds, claims can be sustained under one ground but invalidated under another; small sample sizes for many categories warrant caution in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall outcomes combining DNIs and FWDs (claim survival)
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining Decisions Not to Institute (DNIs) and FWDs, claim survival rates differ: overall ~72% of PGR challenges resulted in no claims being found unpatentable (vs ~60% for IPRs in the data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher claim survival in PGRs is driven by lower institution rates; practitioners should view overall venue favorability by combining institution probability and FWD invalidation rates, not FWD rates alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of PTAB (PGR) vs district court on §112 challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims challenged under §112 have higher survival at the PTAB (PGR) than in district court: e.g., indefiniteness survival 89% at PTAB vs 40% in district court; written description 82% vs 63%; enablement 84% vs 71% (based on included data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is notable because the PTAB uses a lower burden of proof (preponderance) vs district court (clear and convincing), suggesting procedural/venue differences and case-selection effects influence outcomes; sample sizes and case selection should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof difference between PTAB and district court
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB invalidity findings use the preponderance of the evidence standard while district court uses clear and convincing evidence for patent invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the lower PTAB standard, PGR §112 challenges showed higher claim survival at PTAB than district court in the dataset; practitioners must weigh this counter-intuitive empirical result when choosing venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability and standing considerations for challengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of an appeal from a PTAB decision is not guaranteed for challengers because the Federal Circuit has imposed standing requirements for challengers to appeal PTAB decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challengers should consider whether they will have appellate standing before filing a PGR, especially in contexts like biosimilars where early filing (within 9 months) may be too early to confer standing and thus limit appellate remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data limitations and small-sample caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Many PGR subsets (especially life-sciences/biologic and Orange Book PGRs) have small sample sizes, limiting the robustness of trend conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report repeatedly cautions that N is small for several categories (e.g., biologic PGRs N=10; Orange Book N=13) and that trends should be monitored as more PGR decisions accrue; practitioners should avoid over-interpreting small-N patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical decision factors for petitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners must weigh timing constraints, broader estoppel risk, evidentiary burden, institution probability, and potential appealability when deciding whether to file a PGR versus other venues (e.g., IPR or district court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PGRs permit broader statutory challenges but impose estoppel and time/resource demands, petitioners should consider whether they can adequately develop the evidentiary record within nine months post-issuance and whether the risk of estoppel and limited appellate options are acceptable.
